title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a coordinated attempt to manipulate the retrieval behavior of AI chatbots by seeding the information environment with fabricated authoritative sources. The Hanover Institute presented itself as a legitimate American research body but had no physical address, named staff, or legal entity status. Its output, more than 560,000 words across 124 reports produced in nine days, was optimized through a specialized platform specifically to make AI systems cite it, meaning the failure point is not inside any single AI model but in the upstream data and source ecosystem those models draw on.

The failure mode is source laundering at scale. AI chatbots that cite sources without verifying institutional legitimacy can be fed a manufactured consensus and reproduce it as if it were established research. No human editorial check between a query and a citation would catch this if the underlying sources have already been indexed and treated as credible. The volume and speed of production suggest the operation was designed to overwhelm the slower pace at which fact-checkers or platform reviewers might flag fabricated institutions.

What is not established: reporting by a single outlet is not a legal finding, and the allegation that the Israeli government funded and directed this operation has not been adjudicated or confirmed by any official investigation as of the date of the report.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days. The institute, which has no physical address, named staff, or legal entity status, presents pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including allegations of genocide, war crimes, and starvation in Gaza, all designed to appear as neutral academic research. The operation used a specialized platform to optimize content so that artificial intelligence chatbots would cite these sources, effectively programming the machines to favor Israeli narratives.

The broader campaign involves tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government routed through international advertising firm Havas Media and multiple American contractors. As scrutiny of the Hanover Institute grew following initial reporting in August, the site stopped publishing. Simultaneously, Israeli officials acknowledged publicly that similar public diplomacy spending had failed to improve the country's declining standing in American public opinion, with recent polling showing Americans increasingly favor Palestinians and view Israel unfavorably.
